newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania electioneering turns ugly ahead of polls.
newsitem.headline: Romania electioneering turns ugly ahead of polls.

text.p: Romanian police said on Friday they were investigating an anti-Semitic attack on a former prime minister who is trying to oust President Ion Iliescu in an increasingly dirty election campaign.

The incident last week in the western city of Timisoara, labelled Petre Roman as a Jew. Roman and academic Emil Constantinescu lead the field of 15 challengers to Iliescu in the November 3 ballot seen as a watershed for reforms.
"We have launched an investigation to catch these people," Timisoara police spokesman Major Ioan Hada said by telephone.
"We can't agree with this," he said, referring to stickers pasted over Roman's campaign posters in Timisoara by an obscure "Group for Ethnic Conscience."
"Do you want this country to be ruled by a Jew? Then vote for Petre Roman," read the stickers plastered around the city.
Roman's Democratic Party called the incident a desperate attempt by Iliescu's left-wing supporters to cling to power.
"Those who spread the stickers know nothing about this city and its spirit of tolerance. It will turn against them, like a boomerang," local party leader Dorel Borza said from Timisoara.

Latest polls show Iliescu with a healthy lead over Roman and Constantinescu but short of the 50 percent needed for outright victory in the first round. Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) is in second place in the parliamentary vote.
The two-month campaign for president and a two-chamber parliament has thrived on dirty tricks and mudslinging.
Roman has accused Iliescu's campaign of shady ploys to win the elections, the third since the 1989 fall of communism.
"This is the kind of campaign the PDSR and Iliescu are running -- a dirty and poisonous campaign," Roman told the private television station Antena 1 on Thursday.
Vicious barbs have been traded by all the main competitors -- especially on television, the main means of reaching voters in remote rural areas.
Iliescu's campaign clips showed Constantinescu's face fading into a picture of exiled ex-king Michael -- an attempt to brand him a monarchist in a country defined as a republic.
His campaign has portrayed Roman as a criminal, accusing him of squandering millions of dollars from state coffers during his 22-month tenure as prime minister.
Opposition clips juxtapose Iliescu with executed ruler Nicolae Ceausescu in typical Communist-era speechmaking.

Earlier this month, a leading member of the European parliament accused Iliescu's supporters of being poised to rig the outcome, on the heels of a fake telephone survey with loaded questions against Iliescu's rivals.
Iliescu retorted that the opposition was hiring hecklers and paying them up to 60,000 lei (around $20) each per day to jeer him on his campaign trail across Romania.
Roman, whose father was Jewish, was forced from office during riots led by coalminers in September 1991. He later said his demise was a coup by communists opposed to reforms.
After his ouster, he fought anti-Semitic jibes in local newspapers by showing documents on television to prove he had been baptised in Romania's mainstream Orthodox church.
A post-communist constitution adopted in 1991 bans anti-Semitic and fascist activities.
Romania saw Europe's biggest post-war exodus of Jews to Israel and elsewhere. Only 14,000 Jews now live in the Balkan country, most of them elderly.
